evidence.title: Informed Consent Disclosures and Minimum Requirements in AI Clinical Trials: Cross-Sectional Analysis
evidence.outcome: Data handling after participant withdrawal in consent documents
evidence.effect: 51 (44.7%) ICs gave no information, 30 (26.3%) specified data destruction, 29 (25.4%) allowed continued use, only 4 (3.5%) offered participants a choice.
evidence.quote: Data handling protocols after participant withdrawal were inconsistent: 51 (44.7%) ICs provided no information, 30 (26.3%) specified data destruction, 29 (25.4%) allowed continued use, and only 4 (3.5%) offered participants a choice.
evidence.sample_unit: informed consent documents from AI clinical trials

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether consent-management practices keep patient data out of AI systems when consent is absent, denied, or revoked, and the recommendation rests on 20 endorsing sources, mostly commentary. One registry review of 114 AI trial consent documents found that only 4 (3.5%) offered participants a choice about their data after withdrawal.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 5 descriptive review of 114 consent documents. It shows gaps in how AI trials describe data handling after withdrawal, but it does not measure whether granting, verifying, or honoring consent changes actual data use.

In the reviewed consent documents, 51 (44.7%) gave no information on data handling after withdrawal and 29 (25.4%) allowed continued use. These figures suggest that revocation may often go unrecorded or unenforced. No study tests whether a pre-use consent check catches such cases before data enter model training or deployment.

The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use state that HIPAA does not allow some AI uses, such as research, without patient authorization, and that its application to other AI uses is not as clear. NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI guide call for consent withdrawal options. No study shows how health systems meet these expectations.

Only 4 of 114 consent documents (3.5%) let participants decide what happened to their data after they left a trial. Patients who withdraw may assume their data stop being used when the documents permit otherwise. This gap may affect trust, although no study measured patient understanding or trust directly.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that test whether consent-management tools, such as EHR-integrated consent interfaces or automated consent checks, prevent AI use of data from patients who denied or revoked consent, and at what staff and technical cost. Such studies should also measure how often revocations are applied to already trained models and whether patients understand the choices offered.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard study reviewed consent documents rather than patients and reported no data on these groups. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether consent tools reach or work for patients who face language or literacy barriers.
